passage: Rajni, you asked why I keep a plate of sewaiyan aside for Farida's family on Eid, so listen. I am Lokesh, your Nana. When your mother was twenty, she came home glowing about her friend Farida, and I felt fear rising. What will the neighbours say? Will she forget our traditions? I nearly said, "Stop seeing her." Instead, one night at dinner I asked, "What do you like about Farida?" Your mother said, "She never laughs at anyone. When I lost my purse on the train, she gave me her own fare home." I went quiet. That was not a label. That was a person. I still worried, but I invited Farida's family for Diwali, and her mother brought sewaiyan a few months later. My fears lost their sharp edges slowly. Your mother and Farida still speak every Sunday.

qa.q: What did Lokesh ask at dinner instead of saying "Stop seeing her"?
qa.a: He asked, "What do you like about Farida?"

qa.q: What was Lokesh afraid of when Rajni's mother came home glowing about Farida?
qa.a: Lokesh was afraid of what the neighbours would say and that she might forget their traditions.

qa.q: What choice did Lokesh make instead of banning the friendship, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: He asked about Farida and listened, which led to hearing about her kindness and to inviting Farida's family for Diwali.

qa.q: How might Rajni's mother have felt when he asked what she liked about Farida?
qa.a: Probably relieved and heard. She answered warmly with a story about Farida's kindness instead of having to defend her.

grounding: A parent worries about a young adult child's close friend of another faith, and honest conversation about values, not labels, replaces a ban.

passage: Nilesh had learned from a neighbour that his son Bhupen, twenty, spent Eid at his friend Kabir's house. Now the two of them were stuck in the car on the flyover approach, the jam already twenty minutes old, and neither could leave. Nilesh gripped the wheel. "People are talking, Bhupen. They say you're at Kabir's house every week." Bhupen sighed. "Papa, ask me what you actually want to ask." Nilesh swallowed. "I'm afraid you'll drift from us. And I'm afraid of what people will say." "Kabir studied with me every night before my exams," Bhupen said quietly. "He never asked me to change anything, and I don't ask him." Nilesh watched the red brake lights ahead. "Invite Kabir for Diwali," he said finally. "I'd like to meet Kabir properly."

qa.q: Where were Nilesh and Bhupen when they had this talk?
qa.a: They were in the car in a traffic jam on the flyover approach.

qa.q: What is Nilesh afraid of when he grips the wheel?
qa.a: Nilesh is afraid that Bhupen will drift from the family and afraid of what people will say.

qa.q: What turning point led Nilesh to invite Kabir for Diwali?
qa.a: Bhupen answered honestly about what Kabir means to him, that Kabir studied with him and never asked him to change, and Nilesh then spoke about his real fear.

qa.q: How does Bhupen see his friendship with Kabir?
qa.a: As a loyal, mutual friendship based on help and respect: Kabir never asks Bhupen to change anything, and Bhupen does not ask Kabir.

grounding: A parent worries about a young adult child's close friend of another faith, and an honest talk about values leads to an invitation instead of a ban.

passage:
Arnab first noticed the photographs on his son's phone: Tushar, twenty, at an iftar, at a college fest, at a wedding, always with the same friend, Shakeel.
At dinner, Arnab's sister said, "You should be careful. People talk. And what if he starts eating their food, skipping pujo?"
Arnab lay awake that night. He thought of his own father, who had forbidden him a friendship with a Christian boy at school. He had never forgiven him.
The next morning he found Tushar making tea. Instead of warning him, he asked, "This Shakeel, what's he like?"
Tushar looked surprised. "Honest. He covered my hostel fees when my scholarship was late, and wouldn't let me pay him back for months."
Arnab was quiet. Then he said, "Bring him for Durga Pujo. Your mother makes too much bhog anyway."

qa.q: What did Shakeel do when Tushar's scholarship was late?
qa.a: He covered Tushar's hostel fees and wouldn't let him pay him back for months.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling when he lay awake?
qa.a: Arnab felt anxious after his sister's warning, but also torn, remembering how hurt he had been when his own father forbade a friendship.

qa.q: Why did asking about Shakeel work better than a warning?
qa.a: Asking about Shakeel's character let Arnab learn about his values, like honesty and generosity, instead of judging by a religious label.

qa.q: How might Tushar feel when his father invites Shakeel for Durga Pujo?
qa.a: Tushar would probably feel surprised and relieved that his father trusts his friendship.

grounding: A father worries about his son's close friend of another faith, remembers his own hurt, and chooses honest conversation about values over banning.

passage:
"Shalini, who is this Irfan who calls every night?"
"A friend, Amma. From my coding class."
"Just a friend? You laugh on the phone for an hour."
"We laugh because he's funny. Is that a crime?"
"Don't be smart. What will people say? A Muslim boy. Your Paati will have a fit."
"Amma, you haven't asked a single thing about him except his religion."
Silence.
"...Fine. Tell me, then. What is he like?"
"He helps his father at the shop every morning before class. He's the only one who noticed when I was sick and brought notes. He's never once disrespected me."
"Hm."
"You're scared of what people say. I get it. But judge him by that, not his name."
"...Bring him for tea. Saturday. But I'll be watching."
"You can watch all you like, Amma."

qa.q: Where did Shalini meet Irfan?
qa.a: She met him at her coding class.

qa.q: What was Amma feeling when she asked about Irfan?
qa.a: Amma felt anxious and afraid of what people would say and how Paati would react to a Muslim boy.

qa.q: What in Shalini's reply helped change Amma's mind?
qa.a: Shalini pointed out that Amma had asked only about Irfan's religion, then described his values and behaviour, which moved the talk from labels to character.

qa.q: How might Paati see Irfan if she meets him?
qa.a: Paati might first be suspicious because of his faith, but getting to know his kindness could soften her.

grounding: A mother fears her daughter's close friendship with a young man of another faith, and honest talk about values leads her to meet him rather than ban it.

passage:
When my daughter Sunaina started staying over at her friend Grace's house every weekend, I was afraid. I'm Sudha, and I'll be honest about that.
Grace's family goes to church every Sunday. Sunaina, twenty-one, started humming their hymns. My mother-in-law said, "Next she'll convert, and the whole community will laugh at us." I lay awake with that sentence.
I nearly told Sunaina she couldn't go any more. I even rehearsed it.
Instead, I asked her one evening, "What do you like about Grace's family?" She said, "They eat together every night, Ma, and they ask each other about their day. We don't anymore."
That stung. But it was true.
I invited Grace's mother for tea. We talked about our daughters for two hours. We didn't talk about religion at all. We didn't need to.

qa.q: What did Sunaina start humming?
qa.a: Sunaina started humming their hymns.

qa.q: What was Sudha afraid of?
qa.a: Sudha feared Sunaina would convert and that the community would laugh at them, and she lay awake with the mother-in-law's warning.

qa.q: Why was asking Sunaina a question wiser than banning the visits?
qa.a: It revealed what Sunaina valued, family meals and talking, and gave Sudha a chance to connect with Grace's family instead of losing her daughter's trust.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel when her mother invites Grace's mother for tea?
qa.a: Sunaina would probably feel relieved and respected, seeing her mother choose connection over fear.

grounding: A mother fears her daughter's closeness to a family of another faith, and honest conversation about values proves better than banning the friendship.

passage:
Note to myself, Sunday night. Vikas's mother.
Vikas has spent every weekend this month at Zubin's flat. Tonight, when he said he'd be at their Navroz dinner, I heard myself say, "Why always them? What will your Chacha say?" He went quiet and packed his bag anyway.
Honestly, I'm not sure what I'm afraid of. That people will talk. That he'll drift from our pujas.
After he left I phoned Zubin's mother to thank her for feeding him so often. She laughed and said Vikas always asks what their prayers mean and then tells them about ours.
What I did next: when he came home I didn't lecture. I asked what he likes about that family. "They argue about books, Ma, and nobody shouts." I told him I'd been scared of losing our traditions. He said he wasn't planning to lose anything. We're inviting Zubin for Diwali.

qa.q: Which dinner did Vikas say he would be at?
qa.a: He said he'd be at their Navroz dinner.

qa.q: What was Vikas's mother afraid of when she questioned the Navroz dinner?
qa.a: She was worried people would talk and anxious that Vikas would drift from the family's pujas, though she admits she isn't sure of her own fear.

qa.q: What went right when Vikas came home?
qa.a: Instead of banning the friendship or lecturing, she asked what he values in that family and admitted her fear, which opened a talk about values and led to a Diwali invitation.

qa.q: How might Vikas have felt when his mother said "Why always them?"
qa.a: Vikas was probably hurt and frustrated; he went quiet but still packed his bag, showing he would not give up the friendship.

grounding: It illustrates a parent worried about a child's close friendship across faiths who moves from a label to an honest talk about values.
